analysis.one_liner: Cracks down on offshore tax havens, corporate profit-shifting, and tax-avoiding corporate inversions.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it harder for wealthy individuals and multinational corporations to use offshore tax havens. It lets the Treasury restrict dealings with foreign banks and countries that obstruct U.S. tax enforcement, requires large public companies to report their profits and taxes country by country, treats foreign corporations run from the United States as domestic for tax purposes, taxes swap payments sent offshore, tightens rules on corporations that reincorporate abroad to escape U.S. taxes, and imposes anti-money-laundering duties on investment advisers and company formation agents. It never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who ultimately cover the gap left by profits and wealth parked offshore; domestic businesses that compete against companies able to shift income to low-tax jurisdictions; and public services funded by federal taxes. Investors also gain, because country-by-country reporting would show them where companies actually book profits and pay taxes.

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes Treasury to impose special measures — such as restricting correspondent accounts and payment cards — on foreign jurisdictions and financial institutions that are of primary money-laundering concern or significantly impede U.S. tax enforcement [S2].

Creates a rebuttable presumption that U.S. persons who formed, funded, or benefited from offshore entities at banks that do not comply with the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act control those entities, and that money flowing through such accounts is taxable income — shifting the burden of proof in tax cases toward the taxpayer [S3].

Requires companies registered with the SEC to report annually, country by country, their revenues, profits, taxes paid, and employees, giving the public and investors visibility into where profits are booked [S2].

Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic corporations for tax purposes, and tightens the rules on corporate inversions so that foreign acquisitions of U.S. companies with more than 50% U.S. ownership or U.S.-based management remain subject to U.S. taxation [S2].

Closes offshore avoidance channels: deductions cannot offset income from deferred foreign earnings, income shifted through intangible-property transfers is taxed, check-the-box and look-through loopholes are repealed, and interest deductions are limited for foreign-parented groups loaded with domestic debt [S3].
Subjects investment advisers and businesses that form corporations, LLCs, and trusts to anti-money-laundering requirements, closing a route used to hide beneficial ownership [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that shift profits offshore, wealthy individuals using offshore accounts, banks and financial institutions in tax-haven jurisdictions, investment advisers, and company-formation firms. Some compliance costs would fall on U.S. banks and securities firms, which might pass them to customers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals, offshore banks, wealthy account holders

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes new reporting and anti-money-laundering duties on investment advisers and entity-formation agents, and new beneficial-owner reporting on withholding agents and financial institutions, creating compliance costs that financial firms may pass on to customers [S3].

The presumption rules flip the burden of proof for anyone with money in a non-complying offshore institution, requiring clear and convincing evidence to rebut — a remedy that could sweep in some legitimate transactions and raise costs for normal international business [S3].

Restrictions on interest deductions and on transfers of intangible property add complexity to an already complicated international tax code, and critics of such measures argue they raise the cost of operating in the United States for foreign-parented firms [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real and large problem — profits and wealth routed through secrecy jurisdictions so they are never taxed — and its heaviest burdens fall on the actors doing the routing. The compliance costs are genuine, and burden-shifting presumptions can catch some legitimate activity, but the core provisions (country-by-country transparency, inversion rules, closing check-the-box and intangible-transfer loopholes) address practices that currently cost ordinary taxpayers and put onshore businesses at a disadvantage. On balance the design is aggressive but aimed in the right direction.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse, joined by Sen. Jeanne Shaheen and four other Democratic cosponsors, introduced the bill on January 13, 2015 [S1].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; that was the last action of any kind in the entire Congress [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 114th Congress on January 3, 2017, without a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations, offshore financial institutions, and wealthy individuals using tax havens kept the status quo, since no provision of the bill ever became law.

for.name: Sen. Jeanne Shaheen
for.what_they_did: Joined the introduction of the bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (Republican-controlled)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat (one lead sponsor, one co-introducer, and four cosponsors), and the Republican-controlled Finance Committee took no action on the bill; no Republican supported it in the record.

industries.note: The bill would tax income they shift offshore through intangible transfers, check-the-box elections, deferred foreign earnings, and inversion deals, and would force public country-by-country reporting of profits and taxes. Ordinary taxpayers and onshore competitors currently absorb the cost of these practices.

industries.industry: Offshore banks and tax-haven financial institutions
industries.note: Treasury could restrict their access to U.S. correspondent accounts and payment cards if they impede U.S. tax enforcement, and money moving through accounts at non-complying institutions would be presumed taxable income. Their business model depends on the secrecy the bill targets.
Expanded FATCA reporting, beneficial-owner reporting, and burden-shifting presumptions make it much harder and riskier to hold untaxed wealth offshore.

Both would be brought under anti-money-laundering rules, including suspicious-activity reporting and customer identification, ending their role as a lightly supervised gateway for hiding beneficial ownership.

They take on new beneficial-owner and offshore-account reporting duties and penalties for failures, a real compliance cost, but they also benefit from a playing field where offshore competitors cannot undercut them on tax evasion.
